section.title: The Lord Says to My Lord
section.sectionRationale: The most quoted Old Testament passage in the New Testament, this royal psalm reveals a coming King who is also David's Lord, seated at God's own right hand and declared a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, uniting throne and altar in a single figure.
section.thesis: God Himself installs a King who is also a Priest forever, One greater than David who reigns at the LORD's right hand and mediates forever after the order of Melchizedek, a figure the New Testament identifies as Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: Two matched movements built around divine oaths: the LORD's decree enthroning the King at His right hand until every enemy becomes His footstool, verses 1-3, and the LORD's oath establishing Him as a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, who judges the nations in the day of His wrath, verses 4-7.

verses.text: A Psalm of David. The LORD said to my Lord: "Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet."
The LORD extends Your mighty scepter from Zion: "Rule in the midst of Your enemies."
Your people shall be willing on Your day of battle. Arrayed in holy splendor, from the womb of the dawn, to You belongs the {{tal|dew}} of Your youth.

units.label: A priest forever after the order of Melchizedek
units.note: the eternal priest-king, judge of the nations

verses.text: The LORD has sworn and will not change His mind: "You are a {{kohen|priest}} forever in the order of {{malkitzedek|Melchizedek}}."
The Lord is at Your right hand; He will crush kings in the day of His wrath.
He will judge the nations, heaping up the dead; He will crush the leaders far and wide.
He will drink from the brook by the road; therefore He will lift up His head.

tal.gloss: Dew, an image of freshness, vitality, and countless abundance appearing at dawn. The King's youthful army is pictured as numerous and vigorous as morning dew, arrayed in holy splendor for His day of battle.

kohen.gloss: Priest, one who mediates between God and people through sacrifice and intercession. This King is declared a priest by divine oath, a role Israel's law kept strictly separate from kingship, making this figure wholly unique.

malkitzedek.gloss: Melchizedek, meaning king of righteousness, the ancient king-priest of Salem who blessed Abraham, Genesis 14:18-20. The psalm declares the coming King a priest forever after this same rare, pre-Levitical order.

basic.context: David, Israel's king, speaks of another figure he calls 'my Lord,' someone greater than himself, whom God invites to sit at His own right hand and whom God swears by oath to be a priest forever after the pattern of the ancient king-priest Melchizedek.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm is Israel's own king confessing a superior King and Priest to come; Jesus later presses exactly this puzzle on the Pharisees, asking how David's own son could also be David's Lord, Matthew 22:41-45, forcing them to reckon with a Messiah who is more than a mere human descendant.
basic.originalLanguages: God invites this King's Lord to sit at His right hand, the place of shared rule and highest honor, while His army is as numerous and vigorous as tal, morning dew. Most strikingly, God swears by oath that this King is also kohen, priest, forever in the order of Melchizedek, malki tzedeq, uniting throne and altar in one person.
basic.typology: Melchizedek, the king-priest of Salem who had no recorded beginning or end of days in the Genesis narrative, Genesis 14:18-20, foreshadows a priesthood not inherited by bloodline but established by God's own unchangeable oath, a pattern the book of Hebrews unfolds at length concerning Christ.
basic.christ: This is the most quoted Old Testament passage in the New Testament. Jesus applies verse 1 to Himself to press His own deity and Davidic Lordship, Matthew 22:41-45; the apostles read His ascension and enthronement as the fulfillment of sitting at God's right hand, Acts 2:34-35, 1 Corinthians 15:25, Hebrews 1:13; and Hebrews 5 through 7 builds its entire argument for Christ's eternal, unbreakable priesthood on verse 4's oath concerning Melchizedek's order.
basic.god: God Himself speaks and swears, installing this King-Priest by sovereign decree and unbreakable oath, not by human election or hereditary right. He shares His throne with this figure, fights for Him against every hostile king, and secures His priesthood forever by an oath He will not revoke.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 22:41-45 records Jesus using this psalm to press His identity as David's Lord. Acts 2:34-35 applies verse 1 to Christ's ascension and enthronement. Hebrews 5:6, 7:17, and 7:21 build the case for Christ's eternal priesthood directly from verse 4.
basic.oneStory: The King David calls his own Lord is revealed across Scripture to be Jesus Christ, enthroned at God's right hand and declared priest forever by unbreakable oath, so that in Him kingship and priesthood, government and mediation, meet in a single person who reigns now and will one day subdue every enemy, including death itself.

context.literary:
Psalm 110 is one of the shortest royal psalms and one of the most tightly built. It is a poem about two speeches of God, and the psalmist is a listener. Verse 1 opens with a formula that the BSB renders 'The LORD said,' but the Hebrew word is the prophetic term for an oracle, the same word David uses of himself in 2 Samuel 23:1-2, 'The oracle of David son of Jesse ... The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me.' The psalm presents itself as received, not invented.

The first oracle, verses 1 to 3, gives the king a seat, a footstool and a scepter. The second, verse 4, is only one verse long but is the hinge of the whole poem, because it is the only place where God swears. The oracle of verse 1 is a promise; the oracle of verse 4 is an oath. After that the voice changes. From verse 5 the speaker addresses the king again, and the roles reverse: where the king sat at God's right hand in verse 1, now 'the Lord is at Your right hand,' ready to crush kings.

The poem moves in a steady pattern of enthronement, then authority, then war, then rest. It begins with a man sitting down and ends with a man lifting his head, and the whole of the fighting in verses 5 and 6 lies between two postures of calm. Verse 7 is a quiet closing image. After the heaped dead of verse 6, the king stops at a brook, drinks, and raises his head. The war is real, but it is not frantic. There are also three titles hidden in the lines: the king is 'my Lord,' a ruler on Zion, and a priest, and each one is given by God rather than taken.
context.historical:
The first hearers knew this psalm as a song of the Jerusalem monarchy. Zion, verse 2, was the fortress David captured from the Jebusites, 2 Samuel 5:6-9, and the place where he brought up the ark, 2 Samuel 6:17-18. The king ruled from there in God's name, and Psalms such as 2 and 72 show what was said over a new king: nations given as an inheritance, enemies lying low, rule from sea to sea. Psalm 110 belongs to that world of enthronement language, and the line 'Rule in the midst of Your enemies' reminds us that Israel's kings were surrounded by hostile neighbours.

The 'right hand' was the place of honour and of delegated power, and the 'footstool' was a picture every ancient reader understood. Conquered kings were made to lie beneath the conqueror's feet. When Joshua called his commanders to put their feet on the necks of five defeated kings, Joshua 10:24, he acted out exactly the scene the psalm promises. The footstool is also a worship word. The ark and the temple could be called God's footstool, Psalm 99:5 and Psalm 132:7, so the psalm quietly joins the king's rule to the place of God's presence.

The hardest piece of history is verse 4. Israel's law drew a firm line between throne and altar. Priesthood belonged to Aaron's house by a permanent statute, Exodus 29:9, and when King Uzziah forced his way into the temple to burn incense he was struck with leprosy, 2 Chronicles 26:16-20, just as Saul had lost his dynasty after offering sacrifice himself, 1 Samuel 13:8-14. David wore a priestly ephod and blessed the people, 2 Samuel 6:14, 18, but still appointed Zadok and Abiathar as priests, 2 Samuel 8:17. So to a first hearer a king who is also a priest could only be allowed outside the Levitical order, and the psalm says so. It names Melchizedek, a figure from Jerusalem's own past, Genesis 14:18, whose city was called Salem, Psalm 76:2, and whose priesthood lay centuries before Aaron.
context.canonical:
Psalm 110 sits in the middle of the Davidic hope that runs through the Old Testament. God promised David a descendant whose throne would be established forever, 2 Samuel 7:12-16, and swore it, Psalm 89:3-4, 35-37. Psalm 2 gave that king the nations as his inheritance, and Psalm 132:11-12 repeated the oath. Psalm 110 adds the piece that those texts leave out, which is that this king will be a priest, and that his rule will be exercised from God's own side. Zechariah later pictures a man called the Branch who 'will be a priest on His throne,' Zechariah 6:13, with peaceful counsel between the two offices, a text that seems to lean on this psalm.

The New Testament makes more of this psalm than of any other chapter. Its first verse is cited or echoed in Matthew 22:44, Mark 14:62, Luke 22:69, Acts 2:34-35, 1 Corinthians 15:25, Ephesians 1:20-22, Colossians 3:1, Hebrews 1:3, 1:13, 8:1, 10:12-13, 12:2 and 1 Peter 3:22. Its fourth verse is quoted in Hebrews 5:6, 7:17 and 7:21, and Hebrews 7 is in effect a long sermon on a single line of it. At his trial Jesus joined this psalm to Daniel 7:13-14, saying that they would see the Son of Man 'sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven,' Mark 14:62. The high priest tore his clothes, which shows how clearly the claim was heard.

Within the Psalter, Psalm 110 is the last of the great royal psalms before the long run of praise that follows it. It is a psalm that waits: the king is seated until something happens, and the rest of the canon keeps asking when.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm is introduced as David's, and Jesus takes it that way, Matthew 22:43. If so, the author means his own hearers to look past the throne they can see. David is speaking as a prophet, and he reports what God said to someone he calls 'my Lord.' It would be strange for a king to address his own successor like that, since a father does not normally call his son 'lord.' The intent seems to be that Israel should hold its hope for the future king with a certain awe: this son of David will be given a place that David himself does not hold.

The psalm also means to settle a question that the law left open. Israel had a king and a priesthood, and the two kept colliding. By setting a sworn priesthood beside a sworn kingship, the psalm shows that God had a plan in which the two would meet without the old sin of seizing what was not given. The king does not take the priesthood by force, as Uzziah tried to; it is handed to him by a God who has sworn.

Finally, it means to give comfort to a people who lived among enemies. The king who is told to rule 'in the midst of Your enemies' is not safe or quiet, but he is seated, and the one who seated him will do the fighting. The first hearers were meant to trust that the throne was secure even when the evidence was against it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Nothing in this psalm commands the reader to do anything. It records what God said to the king and what God will do for him, so its main weight is promise, and applying it means believing what is said about the King, not copying what he does. The violence of verses 5 and 6 is the clearest example. The crushing of kings is something the Lord does on His own day, and the psalm gives no instruction that His people should make war, so it is a mistake to take these lines as permission for any human army to claim them.

The one phrase that does speak of people is the willingness of verse 3. That is described rather than demanded, but it is not passive, because it shows what the King's people look like when He rules. They come as a freewill offering. The New Testament picks up the priestly side of the psalm and applies it to believers: those who belong to the King are called 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, and made 'a kingdom, priests to His God and Father,' Revelation 1:6. So the psalm shapes how believers think of their access to God and their future with Christ, rather than giving them a list of tasks.

debates.question: Is the psalm about David, a later Davidic king, or the Messiah alone?

views.label: It was written for an ordinary Davidic king and later read messianically
views.case: Many scholars note that the enthronement language, the nations as enemies and the footstool belong to the court style of the monarchy, and that the Hebrew could be an oracle spoken to a reigning king by a court prophet or priest. On that view the psalm was first sung of Israel's kings and was only gradually seen to describe someone greater, because no king in the line ever matched it, least of all in the matter of the priesthood.

views.label: It speaks directly of the Messiah
views.case: The superscription gives the psalm to David, and Jesus argues from that, Matthew 22:43, as does Peter, who says David 'did not ascend into heaven,' Acts 2:34. David is not speaking of himself, because he is addressing someone he calls 'my Lord' and who sits where David never sat. Nothing in the psalm fits any actual king of Judah, who all died, and no king after David was a priest forever.

views.label: It has a double horizon
views.case: A middle view holds that David wrote of the kind of king God would give Israel, and that this language was meant from the start to reach beyond each of David's heirs. Each king was a partial answer, and the psalm kept pointing forward until the one came who fit every line.

debates.bearing: Jesus and the apostles assume that David spoke by the Spirit of a figure greater than himself, and their argument depends on that. A reader can notice the royal setting and still hold that the words reach their full weight only in Christ. Either way the psalm does not describe a king who merely died and was succeeded.

debates.question: Who was Melchizedek, and how does Hebrews use him?

views.label: A historical Canaanite priest-king who pictures Christ
views.case: Genesis 14:18-20 presents Melchizedek as a real king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abram and received a tenth. When Hebrews says he was 'without father or mother or genealogy,' Hebrews 7:3, it is making a point about what the text does not record. Silence about his birth and death is read as a picture of a priesthood that does not depend on descent. On this view Melchizedek is a type, not a heavenly being.

views.label: A pre-incarnate appearance of the Son
views.case: Some readers take the phrase 'without beginning of days or end of life' literally and think Melchizedek was the Son appearing before His birth. They point to Hebrews 7:3, 'like the Son of God,' and to the unusual honour given to him by Abram.

views.label: A heavenly figure from later Jewish tradition
views.case: Some scholars note that later Jewish writings imagined Melchizedek as an exalted heavenly being, and suggest the author of Hebrews knew such ideas. The text of Hebrews itself, however, bases its argument on what Genesis and the psalm say, and not on any outside tradition.

debates.bearing: The wording of Hebrews 7:3 says he is 'like the Son of God,' which puts him in the position of the likeness, not the original. That favours the first view. Whatever one decides, the point stays the same: the psalm promises a priesthood grounded in God's oath and not in tribal descent.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the psalm in Hebrew is neum, usually translated 'oracle' or 'declares.' It is the word that introduces a prophetic utterance throughout the Prophets, as in 'declares the LORD,' and David claims it of himself in 2 Samuel 23:1. The BSB renders it simply 'said,' which loses the sense of solemn disclosure. Psalm 110 begins as revelation, with God as the speaker and the human poet as the hearer.

In the same verse, the two 'Lords' are two different words. The first is the covenant name of God, YHWH, represented in English as LORD in capitals. The second, 'my Lord,' is adoni, the ordinary Hebrew word that a person used for a master or a king, as when Abraham's servant spoke of his master. It is not adonai, the form used for God Himself. This is why Jesus can use the psalm in Matthew 22:43-45: David is addressing someone who is above him but who is not the LORD in the first line. At the same time, the person addressed shares God's throne, and that is why the New Testament goes on to call Jesus 'Lord' in a fuller sense, Acts 2:36.

The word for 'footstool,' hadom, is used of the ark and of the temple as God's footstool in Psalm 99:5 and Psalm 132:7, and it describes conquered enemies here. The picture combines the sanctuary and the battlefield. The verb for 'rule' in verse 2, radah, is the verb used for human dominion over creation in Genesis 1:28, a quiet hint that this king will carry out what humanity was made to do.

Verse 3 is the most difficult verse in the psalm, and the BSB reflects that. 'Your people shall be willing' translates a Hebrew phrase in which the word is the plural of the term for a freewill offering, as in Leviticus 7:16, so the people could be read as 'freewill offerings' themselves on the day of battle. The Septuagint reads the last clause very differently, 'from the womb before the morning star I have begotten you,' which is why some early Christian writers saw the eternal generation of the Son here. The Hebrew 'dew of Your youth' speaks of a fresh and numberless host, and the difference between the two readings shows how old the difficulty is.

Verse 4 uses two solemn verbs. 'Has sworn' is in a form that marks a completed, binding act, and 'will not change His mind' uses the verb nacham, the same verb used in Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 to say that God is not a man who changes His mind. The phrase 'in the order of' translates a Hebrew expression built on the word for 'word' or 'manner,' so it means something like 'after the manner of Melchizedek.' The Septuagint renders it with a word for rank or order, taxis, which Hebrews 5:6 and 7:17 then use. The oath makes the priesthood eternal, and Hebrews 7:20-22 builds on the point that the Levitical priests were appointed without an oath.

typology.type: Melchizedek, king and priest of Salem, Genesis 14:18-20
typology.fulfillment: Melchizedek is the only man in Genesis who is both king and priest, and he blesses Abram with bread and wine. The psalm makes him the pattern for a coming figure, and Hebrews unfolds it: his name means 'king of righteousness,' and 'king of Salem' means 'king of peace,' Hebrews 7:2. Abram's tithe shows that he is greater than the patriarch, and so greater than the Levi who was still in Abram's loins, Hebrews 7:4-10. In Christ the pattern is fulfilled by a priest who 'remains a priest for all time,' Hebrews 7:3. The type falls short in that Melchizedek is only 'like the Son of God,' and we are told nothing of any sacrifice by him.

typology.type: The footstool, enemies beneath the king's feet, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: When Joshua's commanders set their feet on the necks of the five kings, Joshua 10:24, Israel saw what it meant for enemies to lie under a leader's feet. The picture is taken up and enlarged in the New Testament: the Father 'put everything under His feet,' Ephesians 1:22, and Hebrews 10:13 says that Christ 'waits for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet.' The escalation is that the final enemy is not a king but death, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26. The type is not yet complete, since Hebrews 2:8 admits that 'we do not see everything subject to him,' so the footstool belongs partly to the future.

typology.type: The priest who sits down, verse 1 with Hebrews 10:11-12
typology.fulfillment: Israel's priests never sat in the sanctuary. Day after day they stood and offered the same sacrifices, Hebrews 10:11, because the work was never finished. The psalm puts a priest-king in a seat, and the author of Hebrews notices: 'when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God,' Hebrews 10:12. The seat is the proof that the offering was complete. The pattern falls short at the point of repetition, since the old order had no seat, but Christ's session is also an ongoing ministry, because He 'always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25.

typology.type: The brook and the lifted head, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The last line pictures a warrior-king who pauses to drink and then raises his head, the posture of someone who has won. Scripture often joins suffering and exaltation in this way. Paul writes that Christ 'humbled Himself' and that therefore 'God exalted Him to the highest place,' Philippians 2:8-9, and Hebrews 12:2 says that Jesus 'endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.' Some readers think the brook speaks of a humbled path before triumph. That is only a suggestion, since the verse is brief and obscure, and the typology here is held loosely.

study.christ:
No chapter of the Old Testament is turned to Christ more often or more directly than this one, and the New Testament gives its own reasons. It starts with Jesus Himself. In the temple He asks the Pharisees whose son the Christ is, and when they say David's, He asks how David 'in the Spirit' can call Him Lord, Matthew 22:41-45. The question is not a trick. It exposes that they hold only half of the truth, a son of David without a Lord of David. 'No one was able to answer a word,' Matthew 22:46.

Peter makes the argument at Pentecost. David died and was buried, 'for David did not ascend into heaven,' Acts 2:34, so the words of Psalm 110 can only describe the risen Jesus, who has been 'exalted to the right hand of God,' Acts 2:33. The psalm moves from private prophecy to public proclamation. 'God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ,' Acts 2:36. The seat at the right hand is the ascension, and that seat is where the New Testament places Christ's present rule, Ephesians 1:20-22, Colossians 3:1 and 1 Peter 3:22. Stephen sees Him there standing, Acts 7:55-56, and Paul says that He is interceding for us, Romans 8:34.

Hebrews takes up verse 4 and builds the doctrine of Christ's priesthood from it. Christ 'did not take upon Himself the glory of becoming a high priest' but was called, Hebrews 5:5-6. He is a priest 'not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life,' Hebrews 7:16. Because the old priests died, they were many; because Jesus lives forever, 'He has a permanent priesthood,' Hebrews 7:23-24. He is the 'guarantee of a better covenant,' Hebrews 7:22, and 'able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him,' Hebrews 7:25. The oath came after the law and appointed 'the Son, who has been made perfect forever,' Hebrews 7:28.

The two offices belong together in the psalm, and the gospel shows why. A king without a priest can only judge, and a priest without a king can only plead. In Jesus the one who rules is the one who bore sin, and the one who bore sin is the one who rules, so His throne is also a throne of grace, Hebrews 4:14-16. The fighting of verses 5 and 6 is taken up in Revelation 19:11-16, where the rider on the white horse strikes the nations with a sharp sword and carries the name King of kings. The psalm has two sides, mercy now and judgment later, and both belong to the same Lord.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The psalm is not a code. The New Testament does not tell us what the brook of verse 7 means, and it would be a mistake to claim a precise meaning for the dew or the womb of the dawn. The firm links are those the apostles themselves draw: the seat, the footstool, the oath and the priesthood.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm shows about God is that He speaks in order to install. The king is not self-made. In the opening verses the LORD gives him a seat, a scepter, a footstool and an army, and the king's only action in verse 1 is to sit. The picture of God here is of a sovereign who delegates His own rule without lessening it. The LORD extends the scepter, verse 2, and the LORD does the work of the footstool, verse 1, 'until I make Your enemies a footstool.' The King shares God's throne, but the strength is God's.

He is a God who swears. When God takes an oath it is because He wants His people to be certain. Hebrews says that when God wanted to make 'the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear' to the heirs of the promise, 'He guaranteed it with an oath,' Hebrews 6:17. The line 'will not change His mind' stands next to other passages where God does relent, as in Exodus 32:14, and the two are not in conflict. God changes His course when a person repents, but He does not change His promise. His plans for His chosen king, and for the salvation that king brings, are fixed.

He is a God of judgment. Verses 5 and 6 are bracing: kings crushed, nations judged, the dead heaped up. It would be easy to skip over these lines, but a psalm that spoke only of mercy would not describe the God who is just. The wrath is directed at rulers who stand against the King and against His people, and it is described as His 'day of wrath,' belonging to God's time and not to ours. The God of this psalm does not leave evil unanswered. The same God appoints a priest, so that there is a way of mercy while the judgment waits.

He is also a God who joins things that Israel's law had kept apart. The separation of king and priest was a gift, because it protected both offices from pride. Yet the oath of verse 4 shows that the separation was a provision for a time, and that God Himself had planned a priest-king. The God of Psalm 110 is neither careless with His own laws nor bound by them in a way that stops Him from fulfilling them in someone greater.

For worship, this means that the believer can pray and sing with confidence that the throne is occupied. The psalm does not ask us to defeat the enemies of God. It invites us to trust that the one who sits at His right hand reigns now, intercedes now, and will finish what He began, and to bring ourselves, as the freewill offerings of verse 3, to Him.

crossReferences.note: Jesus cites verse 1 to show that the Christ is both David's son and David's Lord. The question silences His opponents because it forces them to see that David, speaking by the Spirit, called his own descendant 'Lord.'

Peter reasons that David did not ascend into heaven, so the words of verse 1 must describe Jesus, raised and exalted. The psalm becomes the framework of the first Christian sermon, ending with 'both Lord and Christ.'

The author joins Psalm 2:7 and Psalm 110:4 to show that Christ did not seize the priesthood but was called to it by God. The one who learned obedience through suffering is designated high priest in Melchizedek's order.

The longest exposition of verse 4. A priest who lives by an indestructible life makes the old succession unnecessary, and the oath of verse 4 makes this priesthood a guarantee of a better covenant that can save completely.

The only earlier scene with Melchizedek, who brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram and receives a tenth. The psalm takes this brief meeting and treats it as the pattern for a priesthood of a different kind.

Paul draws on verse 1 and says that Christ 'must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet,' and names death as the last enemy. The footstool of the psalm is given a specific and final opponent.

A parallel royal psalm: God installs His king on Zion and gives him the nations. Both psalms speak of a decree, of Zion, and of enemies broken, and the New Testament links them for the same Christ in Hebrews 5:5-6.
The covenant promise of a descendant whose throne will be established forever. Psalm 110 enlarges it by showing that the heir will sit at God's right hand and will also be a priest.

The Branch builds the temple and 'will be a priest on His throne,' with peace between the two offices. The prophet gives the same combination of throne and priesthood, and applies it to a coming figure.

Uzziah entered the temple to burn incense and was struck with leprosy. The story shows why a king-priest was unthinkable under the law, and so how startling the oath of Psalm 110:4 would have sounded.
Jesus answers the high priest by joining Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13. The high priest tears his clothes at the claim, which shows that he heard the psalm as a claim to share God's throne.

The rider who judges and makes war carries the sharp sword and treads the winepress of God's wrath, and wears the name King of kings. The warfare of verses 5 and 6 is shown as the work of Christ at the end.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with a king and a priest who fail. Adam was made to rule the creation, Genesis 1:28, and to keep the garden, Genesis 2:15, a work that includes both dominion and priestly care. He lost both when he listened to the serpent. Psalm 110 is part of God's answer, because it describes a man who is given the rule and the priesthood together and who does not lose them.

Through the Old Testament the two offices are separated and both fail. Israel's kings repeat Adam's grasping, and its priests, even in the line of Aaron, die and leave the work unfinished. The prophets keep watching for something better: a shoot from David's line, a servant who bears sin and makes intercession, Isaiah 53:12, a Branch who is a priest on his throne, Zechariah 6:13. Psalm 110 is the song that holds those hopes together and gives them an oath.

In the New Testament the psalm is fulfilled in stages. Christ is raised, ascends, and sits down at God's right hand, so the footstool has begun to take effect. His people are made 'a kingdom, priests,' Revelation 1:5-6, which restores in them something of Adam's lost calling. Meanwhile He waits, as Hebrews 10:13 puts it, for the enemies to be made His footstool. Paul says that the last of them is death, 1 Corinthians 15:26.

The story ends where the psalm points. In Revelation the King returns with armies, and the nations are judged. The one who sits on the throne shares it with those who overcome, Revelation 3:21, and the kingdom is handed to the Father, 1 Corinthians 15:24. In the new creation there is no temple because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22, and the priest and the king are one. Psalm 110 is the promise that this ending is not a hope for an ideal ruler but an oath sworn by God.

sermon.title: The True King
sermon.why: Keller works through Psalm 110:1-7 as the most quoted Old Testament passage in the New Testament, showing how it presents a King who combines excellencies never combined in a single figure, divine and human, strong yet weak, and how Jesus Himself used this psalm to explain who He is.

quiz.q: What does the LORD invite David's Lord to do in verse 1?

options.text: Sit at His right hand until his enemies become a footstool for his feet.
options.note: This is the enthronement the New Testament repeatedly applies to Christ's ascension and reign.

options.text: Go and personally destroy every enemy at once.
options.note: The psalm depicts a period of reigning at God's right hand before enemies are fully subdued, not instant destruction.

options.text: Remain hidden until all opposition disappears on its own.
options.note: The King is seated in a place of active honor and rule, not hidden away.

options.text: Return to Zion to await further instructions.
options.note: The scepter is extended from Zion, verse 2, but the King's own place is at God's right hand, not merely awaiting orders in Zion.

quiz.q: According to verse 4, by what means is this King also declared a priest?

options.text: By the LORD's own unchangeable oath, forever, after the order of Melchizedek.
options.note: This divine oath is the very basis of Hebrews' argument for Christ's eternal priesthood.

options.text: By inheriting the office from the line of Aaron.
options.note: The order named is Melchizedek's, explicitly distinct from the Aaronic, Levitical priesthood.

options.text: By popular vote among the priests of Israel.
options.note: The priesthood is established by God's own oath, not by any human vote or election.

options.text: By a temporary appointment lasting only David's lifetime.
options.note: The text explicitly says forever, not a temporary or lifetime appointment.

quiz.q: How does Jesus Himself use this psalm in Matthew 22:41-45?

options.text: He presses that the Messiah must be more than David's son, since David calls Him Lord.
options.note: Jesus uses verse 1 to show the Messiah's identity exceeds mere human descent from David.

options.text: He denies that the psalm has any messianic meaning.
options.note: Jesus affirms and applies the psalm's messianic significance directly to Himself.

options.text: He uses it to prove His descent from the tribe of Levi.
options.note: The point is precisely the opposite; this priesthood stands outside the Levitical line, after Melchizedek's order.

options.text: He uses it only to criticize the Pharisees' fasting practices.
options.note: The confrontation concerns the identity of the Messiah as David's Lord, not fasting practices.

quiz.q: What does Melchizedek's order signify about the priesthood described in verse 4?

options.text: A priesthood established by God's oath rather than by hereditary Levitical descent.
options.note: Hebrews 7 draws out exactly this contrast between Melchizedek's order and the Levitical priesthood.

options.text: A priesthood limited strictly to offering grain offerings.
options.note: The text does not restrict this priesthood's function in this way; the point is its unique, non-Levitical basis.

options.text: A priesthood that ended when Melchizedek died.
options.note: The point of the typology, developed in Hebrews, is a priesthood without the interruption of hereditary succession.

options.text: A priesthood reserved only for foreign nations, never for Israel's king.
options.note: The psalm applies this very priesthood to Israel's own coming King, not to a foreign nation exclusively.

quiz.q: How do the apostles apply verse 1 concerning Christ's present reign?

options.text: They teach He is now seated at God's right hand, reigning until all His enemies, including death, are subdued.
options.note: Acts 2:34-35, 1 Corinthians 15:25, and Hebrews 1:13 all apply this verse to Christ's present session and ongoing reign.

options.text: They teach the enthronement described here has not yet begun.
options.note: The apostles teach Christ's session at God's right hand began at His ascension and continues now.

options.text: They apply it only to a future earthly throne in Jerusalem, not to Christ's current reign.
options.note: The New Testament applies this to Christ's present heavenly session, not merely to a future earthly throne.

options.text: They apply it exclusively to the future final judgment, with no present significance.
options.note: The apostles teach this reign is already underway now, even as it moves toward a final subduing of every enemy.

questions: David confesses a King greater than himself, one he calls Lord. How does recognizing Jesus as both fully human and fully divine, both son of David and Lord of David, shape the way you worship Him this week?

This King reigns now at God's right hand even while enemies still exist and must be subdued over time. Where do you need to trust that Christ is already reigning, even in a situation that does not yet look fully resolved?

Christ's priesthood, sworn forever after the order of Melchizedek, means His intercession for you never lapses or needs renewal. How does knowing you have a permanent, unfailing Priest change how you approach God in prayer today?
The psalm unites kingship and priesthood, government and mediation, in a single figure. Where in your life do you need both Christ's authority to rule and His priestly mediation to draw near to God?
David's people are described as willing volunteers on the day of battle. What would it look like for you to serve Christ's kingdom as a willing volunteer this week rather than out of mere obligation?

translationNotes.note: The LORD said to my Lord translates two distinct Hebrew words, Yahweh, God's covenant name, and Adonai, Lord, David's title for the superior figure he describes, a distinction Jesus presses in Matthew 22:41-45.
The dew of Your youth pictures the King's people as fresh, numerous, and vigorous as morning dew, gathered willingly on His day of battle, arrayed in holy splendor.

In the order of Melchizedek recalls the king-priest of Salem in Genesis 14:18-20, whose office, unlike the Levitical priesthood, was not established by hereditary descent but stands as a type of a priesthood without beginning or end of days, Hebrews 7:3.
